cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SaltStack Salt Path Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SaltStack Salt contains a path traversal vulnerability in the salt-master process ClearFuncs which allows directory access to authenticated users. Salt users who follow fundamental internet security guidelines and best practices are not affected by this vulnerability.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SaltStack Salt Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SaltStack Salt contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the salt-master process ClearFuncs due to improperly validating method calls. The vulnerability allows a remote user to access some methods without authentication, which can be used to retrieve user tokens from the salt master and/or run commands on salt minions. Salt users who follow fundamental internet security guidelines and best practices are not affected by this vulnerability.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SaltStack Salt Shell Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SaltStack Salt allows an unauthenticated user with network access to the Salt API to use shell injections to run code on the Salt API using the SSH client. This vulnerability affects any users running the Salt API.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP Customer Relationship Management (CRM) Path Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP Customer Relationship Management (CRM) contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows an attacker to exploit insufficient validation of path information provided by users.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms Invoker Servlet does not require authentication, allowing for remote code execution via a HTTP or HTTPS request.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver XML External Entity (XXE) Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms contains an unspecified vulnerability in BC-BMT-BPM-DSK which allows remote, authenticated users to conduct XML External Entity (XXE) attacks.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms contains a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability allowing unauthenticated access to execute configuration tasks and create administrative users.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP Solution Manager Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP Solution Manager User Experience Monitoring contains a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability which results in complete compromise of all SMDAgents connected to the Solution Manager.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SAP NetWeaver Directory Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SAP NetWeaver Application Server Java Platforms contains a directory traversal vulnerability via a ..\ (dot dot backslash) in the fileName parameter to CrashFileDownloadServlet. This allows remote attackers to read files.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SIMalliance Toolbox Browser Command Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SIMalliance Toolbox Browser contains an command injection vulnerability that could allow remote attackers to retrieve location and IMEI information or execute a range of other attacks by modifying the attack message.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SolarWinds Orion Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SolarWinds Orion API contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to execute API commands.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SolarWinds Serv-U Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SolarWinds Serv-U contains an unspecified memory escape vulnerability which can allow for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SolarWinds Virtualization Manager Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SolarWinds Virtualization Manager allows for privilege escalation through leveraging a misconfiguration of sudo.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Sonatype Nexus Repository Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Sonatype Nexus Repository contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall Email Security Improper Privilege Management Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall Email Security contains an improper privilege management vulnerability that allows an attacker to create an administrative account by sending a crafted HTTP request to the remote host. This vulnerability has known usage in a SonicWall Email Security exploit chain along with CVE-2021-20022 and CVE-2021-20023 to achieve privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall SMA100 SQL Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall SMA100 contains a SQL injection vulnerability allowing an unauthenticated user to gain read-only access to unauthorized resources.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall Email Security Unrestricted Upload of File Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall Email Security contains an unrestricted upload of file with dangerous type vulnerability that allows a post-authenticated attacker to upload a file to the remote host. This vulnerability has known usage in a SonicWall Email Security exploit chain along with CVE-2021-20021 and CVE-2021-20023 to achieve privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall Email Security Path Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall Email Security contains a path traversal vulnerability that allows a post-authenticated attacker to read files on the remote host. This vulnerability has known usage in a SonicWall Email Security exploit chain along with CVE-2021-20021 and CVE-2021-20022 to achieve privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: SonicWall SSLVPN SMA100 SQL Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: SonicWall SSLVPN SMA100 contains a SQL injection vulnerability that allows remote exploitation for credential access by an unauthenticated attacker.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Sophos SFOS SQL Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Sophos Firewall operating system (SFOS) firmware contains a SQL injection vulnerability when configured with either the administration (HTTPS) service or the User Portal is exposed on the WAN zone. Successful exploitation may cause remote code execution to exfiltrate usernames and hashed passwords for the local device admin(s), portal admins, and user accounts used for remote access (but not external Active Directory or LDAP passwords).
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Sumavision EMR Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Sumavision Enhanced Multimedia Router (EMR) contains a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) vulnerability allowing the creation of users with elevated privileges as administrator on a device.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Symantec Messaging Gateway Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Symantec Messaging Gateway contains an unspecified vulnerability which can allow for remote code execution. With the ability to perform remote code execution, an attacker may also desire to perform privilege escalating actions.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: TeamViewer Desktop Bypass Remote Login Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: TeamViewer Desktop allows for bypass of remote-login access control because the same AES key is used for different customers' installations. If an attacker were to know this key, they could decrypt protected information stored in registry or configuration files or decryption of the Unattended Access password to the system (which allows for remote login to the system).
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX and Sitefinity Cryptographic Weakness Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Progress Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX and Sitefinity have a cryptographic weakness in Telerik.Web.UI.dll that can be exploited to disclose encryption keys (Telerik.Web.UI.DialogParametersEncryptionKey and/or the MachineKey), perform cross-site-scripting (XSS) attacks, compromise the ASP.NET ViewState, and/or upload and download files.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Tenda AC11 Router Stack Buffer Overflow Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Tenda AC11 devices contain a stack buffer overflow vulnerability in /goform/setmac which allows attackers to execute code via a crafted post request.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Tenda AC1900 Router AC15 Model Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Tenda AC1900 Router AC15 Model contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows remote attackers to execute system commands via the deviceName POST parameter.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Tenda AC7, AC9, and AC10 Routers Command Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Tenda AC7, AC9, and AC10 devices contain a command injection vulnerability due to  the "formsetUsbUnload" function executes a dosystemCmd function with untrusted input. Successful exploitation allows an attacker to execute OS commands via a crafted goform/setUsbUnload request.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: ThinkPHP "noneCms" Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: ThinkPHP "noneCms" contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows for remote code execution through crafted use of the filter parameter.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: ThinkPHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: ThinkPHP contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows for remote code execution via public//?s=index/\think\app/invokefunction&function=call_user_func_array&vars[0]=system&vars[1][]= followed by the command.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro OfficeScan Directory Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro OfficeScan contains a directory traversal vulnerability by extracting files from a zip file to a specific folder on the OfficeScan server, leading to remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Apex One and OfficeScan Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro Apex One and OfficeScan contain an unspecified vulnerability within a migration tool component that allows for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.product: Apex One, OfficeScan and Worry-Free Business Security Agents
cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Multiple Products Content Validation Escape Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro Apex One, OfficeScan, and Worry-Free Business Security agents contain a content validation escape vulnerability that could allow an attacker to manipulate certain agent client components.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.product: Apex One, OfficeScan, and Worry-Free Business Security
cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Multiple Products Improper Access Control Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro Apex One, OfficeScan, and Worry-Free Business Security on Microsoft Windows contain an improper access control vulnerability that may allow an attacker to manipulate a particular product folder to disable the security temporarily, abuse a specific Windows function, and attain privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Apex One and OfficeScan Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro Apex One and OfficeScan server contain a vulnerable EXE file that could allow a remote attacker to write data to a path on affected installations and bypass root login.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.product: Apex One, Apex One as a Service, and Worry-Free Business Security
cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Multiple Products Improper Input Validation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro Apex One, Apex One as a Service, and Worry-Free Business Security contain an improper input validation vulnerability that allows for privilege escalation.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.product: Apex One, Apex One as a Service, and Worry-Free Business Security
cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Trend Micro Multiple Products Improper Input Validation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Trend Micro Apex One, Apex One as a Service, and Worry-Free Business Security contain an improper input validation vulnerability that allows a remote attacker to upload files.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: TVT NVMS-1000 Directory Traversal Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: TVT devices utilizing NVMS-1000 software contain a directory traversal vulnerability via GET /.. requests.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Unraid Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Unraid contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that allows attackers to gain access to the administrative interface. This CVE is chainable with CVE-2020-5847 for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Unraid Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Unraid contains a vulnerability due to the insecure use of the extract PHP function that can be abused to execute remote code as root. This CVE is chainable with CVE-2020-5849 for initial access.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: vBulletin PHP Module Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: The PHP module within vBulletin contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows for remote code execution via the widgetConfig[code] parameter in an ajax/render/widget_php routestring request.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: vBulletin PHP Module Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: The PHP module within vBulletin contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows for remote code execution via crafted subWidgets data in an ajax/render/widget_tabbedcontainer_tab_panel request. This CVE ID resolves an incomplete patch for CVE-2019-16759.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware ESXi and Horizon DaaS OpenSLP Heap-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware ESXi and Horizon Desktop as a Service (DaaS) OpenSLP contains a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability that allows an attacker with network access to port 427 to overwrite the heap of the OpenSLP service to perform remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware ESXi OpenSLP Use-After-Free Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware ESXi OpenSLP contains a use-after-free vulnerability that allows an attacker residing in the management network with access to port 427 to perform remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware Multiple Products Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware Fusion, Remote Console (VMRC) for Mac, and Horizon Client for Mac contain a privilege escalation vulnerability due to improper use of setuid binaries that allows attackers to escalate privileges to root.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware vCenter Server File Upload Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware vCenter Server contains a file upload vulnerability in the Analytics service that allows a user with network access to port 443 to execute code.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware vCenter Server Information Disclosure Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware vCenter Server contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service (vmdir) when the Platform Services Controller (PSC) does not correctly implement access controls. Successful exploitation allows an attacker with network access to port 389 to extract sensitive information.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware vCenter Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware vCenter Server vSphere Client contains a remote code execution vulnerability in a vCenter Server plugin which allows an attacker with network access to port 443 to execute commands with unrestricted privileges on the underlying operating system.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: VMware vCenter Server Improper Input Validation Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware vSphere Client contains an improper input validation vulnerability in the Virtual SAN Health Check plug-in, which is enabled by default in vCenter Server, which allows for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Multiple VMware Products Command Injection Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: VMware Workspace One Access, Access Connector, Identity Manager, and Identity Manager Connector contain a command injection vulnerability. An attacker with network access to the administrative configurator on port 8443 and a valid password for the configurator administrator account can execute commands with unrestricted privileges on the underlying operating system.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: WordPress File Manager Plugin Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: WordPress File Manager plugin contains a remote code execution vulnerability that allows unauthenticated users to execute PHP code and upload malicious files on a target site.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: WordPress Snap Creek Duplicator Plugin File Download Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: WordPress Snap Creek Duplicator plugin contains a file download vulnerability when an administrator creates a new copy of their site that allows an attacker to download the generated files from their Wordpress dashboard. This vulnerability affects Duplicator and Dulplicator Pro.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: WordPress Social Warfare Plugin Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: WordPress Social Warfare plugin contains a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability that allows for remote code execution. This vulnerability affects Social Warfare and Social Warfare Pro.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Yealink Device Management Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Yealink Device Management contains a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Zoho ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Zoho ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus contains an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the REST API URLs which allow for remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Zoho ManageEngine Desktop Central File Upload Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Zoho ManageEngine Desktop Central contains a file upload vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Zoho ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus (SDP) File Upload Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Zoho ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus (SDP) contains an unspecified vulnerability that allows remote users to upload files via login page customization.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

cisa_kev_catalog.vulnerabilityName: Zyxel Multiple Products Use of Hard-Coded Credentials Vulnerability
cisa_kev_catalog.shortDescription: Zyxel firewalls (ATP, USG, VM) and AP Controllers (NXC2500 and NXC5500) contain a use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in an undocumented account ("zyfwp") with an unchangeable password.
cisa_kev_catalog.requiredAction: Apply updates per vendor instructions.

items.title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension
items.summary: The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's email service. [...]
items.details:
The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's email service.

On November 8, the Remus infostealer developer started advertising the alleged Gmail zero-day flaw that allowed the malware to collect emails even if victims changed their passwords and revoked all sessions.

Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock investigated the claims but came to inconclusive results. The researchers noted that evidence from the malware customers matched the seller's pitch, although there was no technical proof that a zero-day vulnerability was being exploited.

GenDigital and Invoke RE researchers published their independent findings yesterday, explaining that the advertised “zero-day” was just a malicious Chrome extension installed on the victims' browsers.

The extension is designed to steal unread emails from signed-in Gmail accounts. It can also survive password changes and session revocations because it remains installed in the victim's Chrome browser.

Its access to Gmail stops when the active session ends, and resumes again when the victim signs back in.

GenDigital discovered the extension after reverse-engineering the Remus infostealer. The researchers found no trace of an email-stealing module, suggesting that the functionality is implemented via an add-on.

“In a nutshell, the loaded module is a native DLL whose sole purpose is to install a malicious extension into Google Chrome, which, notably, is the only browser it targets,” GenDigital explains .

“The extension itself is bundled directly inside the DLL, stored as an unencrypted ZIP archive in its .rdata section.”

GenDigital explains that Chrome versions 137 and later removed a command-line option that allowed malware to load extensions.

Remus takes a complex route to overcome this restriction, editing the victim’s Chrome profile to register the malicious extension and then enabling ‘Developer Mode’ in the browser, which is required to run unpacked extensions.

The extension uses the name “Google Sheets,” copies the description of Google Docs Offline, and requests access to all websites.

Once active in the browser, it checks for unread emails every minute across up to 10 account slots and retrieves them in full, in raw format.

The extension sends the email subject, message body, sender, and victim’s email address to its command-and-control server, along with a campaign identifier.

Failed uploads are queued and retried, while a local record helps the extension keep track of what has succeeded so it doesn’t send duplicates.

Although the extension also parses attachment filenames, it does not send those to its operators, so this feature may not be fully implemented yet.

To defend against this threat, users are advised to download software only from trusted sources and scrutinize “chrome://extensions” for rogue installations or unexpected activation of Developer Mode.

technology_background.what_does_it_do: The extension is designed to steal unread emails from signed-in Gmail accounts.

items.details:
SafeDep found a PolinRider Python loader in 375 GitHub repositories that uses Ethereum transactions to retrieve and execute JavaScript.

The threat actors behind the PolinRider campaign have been observed planting a Python loader in GitHub repositories, as evidence emerges that the activity may have started as far back as February 2025.

"The loader hides in a small utils package or in conftest.py," SafeDep said in a report published this week. "When Python imports the file, the loader reads the newest transaction that an Ethereum wallet sent to itself. It decodes the input data of that transaction as JavaScript and runs it with Node.js."

The JavaScript code, for its part, reads a second wallet to locate the command-and-control (C2) server and then passes the next stage to a detached interactive Node.js environment by means of a node -i process.

The software supply chain security company said it identified the loader in 375 public repositories that belong to 260 accounts. There is no evidence that the loader has been distributed via PyPI or npm.

PolinRider is the name assigned to a malicious campaign linked to North Korean threat actors. Recent reports indicate that the activity employs various channels to distribute malware, including -

Fraudulent recruitment campaigns that make use of phishing emails and fake hiring portals like BlockNovas , AccuraSoftHire ("accurasofthire[.]com") and HuntRole ("huntrole[.]org") to trick prospective targets into running malware-laced projects under the pretext of a take-home assessment.

Publishing malicious packages across open-source ecosystems by hijacking maintainer accounts to plant obfuscated malware through fake font files ( fa-solid-400.woff2 , fa-solid-500.woff2, or fa-solid-300.llf ), Visual Studio Code (VS Code) auto-run tasks, and Git history rewriting.

Using compromised developer machines to steal their GitHub tokens and force-push malicious commits into open-source repositories they have access to.

At a high level, the PolinRider loader retrieves an encrypted second-stage Node.js payload that scans the infected host for installed developer applications, such as GitHub Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and Google Antigravity, and tampers with the most frequently used tools to execute attacker-controlled code and deliver infostealer malware.

It's worth noting here that PolinRider is assessed to be a sub-cluster operating in parallel with a long-running campaign codenamed Contagious Interview . While the latter is more of a social-engineering entry point that's used to compromise developer systems, PolinRider abuses the access to modify repositories and turn them into a distribution channel for malware.

"Cybercriminal groups deploy supply chain worms for opportunistic theft. On the other hand, North Korean state-sponsored threat actors use open-source software registries as a primary initial access vector targeting corporate environments," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said in a report published last month.

"Threat actors demonstrate how compromising a single maintainer account or registry scope converts open-source dependencies, resulting in widespread affected cloud environments."

Some of the decoy sites have been found to incorporate two other alternate delivery paths -

Instruct candidates to sideload a Google Chrome extension after enabling "Developer mode" to subscribe to new job alerts.

Employ ClickFix-style lures to get victims to copy and paste malicious commands into the terminal app depending on the operating system as part of a "standard settings bundle for candidates and interview workflows."

"The [job] application asks for a short verification video," StepSecurity said . "Until the server marks a candidate as having installed a 'driver,' the camera check always fails with a message saying the system does not have a compatible camera environment."

"A separate 'Technical onboarding' page on the site gives a one-line curl command to download the 'driver.' On Windows, the downloaded installer fetches a script from the careers site that installs Node.js if it is missing, downloads a JavaScript payload, runs it in the background and deletes itself. The macOS and Linux versions do the same."

items.title: USN-9212-1: PyJWT vulnerabilities
items.summary: It was discovered that PyJWT incorrectly handled errors when parsing deeply nested token headers. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using PyJWT to fail unexpectedly, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-102265) It was discovered that PyJWT modified the options mapping supplied by an application when signature verification was disabled. If an application reused that mapping for a later call with signature verification enabled, an attacker could possibly use this issue to bypass token claim checks, such as expiration. This issue only affected Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-103001)

items.title: SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook
items.summary: A new version of the SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management to force the installation of an extension that steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails. [...]
items.details:
A new version of the SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management to force the installation of an extension that steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails.

The ads lure Windows users into downloading free animated wallpapers that work as advertised but also deploy malware in the background during installation.

The campaign targets Facebook and Meta business accounts and gives the operator access to recent Gmail and Outlook messages in Chrome, and the ability to permanently delete emails.

Bitdefender Labs tracks the campaign as SYS010 and says the malware is likely a new version of the SYS01 infostealer , observed since at least 2022 in malvertising activity on Facebook .

The name reflects the researchers' assessment that this variant represents a major improvement over its predecessor, leading them to tag it as version 2, represented in binary as 010.

Researchers identified a malicious SYS010 ad on October 16 and found that the campaign was still ongoing, with hundreds of ads created.

Company telemetry shows that requests to the threat actor’s servers came from several countries in Asia, Europe, North America, Africa, and South America.

Meta Ad Library' transparency page shows that one advertisement alone reached 6,275 users in the European Union, targeting anyone above 18.

In a report today, Bitdefender says most requests came from the Philippines, Thailand, Bangladesh, Poland, Mexico, Algeria, Belgium, Mongolia, and the United States, but emphasizes these figures do not reflect confirmed infections.

The ads impersonate the legitimate Wallpaper Engine (a renamed, digitally signed version of the MeisterTask desktop app built on Electron) and Lively Wallpapers applications, directing users to malicious download sites, some of them using domains designed to appear official.

After installing the malicious Windows app, users get the advertised animated wallpaper functionality, which helps disguise the malware running in the background.

According to Bitdefender researchers, the attacker forces Chrome, Edge, and Firefox to install malicious browser add-ons by abusing management tools designed for organizations.

A script named eclient.php is responsible for installing the malicious extensions by modifying browser management policies.

In Chrome, it enrolls the browser in an attacker-controlled Google admin console, allowing forced installation of extensions.

In Firefox, it uses an ExtensionSettings policy to force-install an add-on while disabling Developer Tools and abuse reporting.

For Edge, it can enroll the victim's Windows device in an attacker-controlled mobile device management (MDM) server to enable forced extension installation.

These changes require administrator permissions, which is solved by triggering the User Account Control (UAC) prompt and repeating it every three seconds up to 99 times until the user approves the action.

items.title: Most Wanted: The Phishing Kits and Techniques Getting Past Security Controls
items.summary: Every phishing attack has to get past email security, web filtering, and safe browsing before it reaches an employee. Some kits manage that far more often than others, and those are the kits that security teams need to know about. At Push Security, we measure this as breakthrough rate: The share of attacks that get past email security, web gateways, and safe browsing to reach the user. How an
items.details:
Push Security reports DOMDIFFER led phishing kit breakthrough rates from August to October 2026, targeting corporate Google and Microsoft accounts.

Every phishing attack has to get past email security, web filtering, and safe browsing before it reaches an employee. Some kits manage that far more often than others, and those are the kits that security teams need to know about.

At Push Security, we measure this as breakthrough rate : The share of attacks that get past email security, web gateways, and safe browsing to reach the user.

Every browser-based attack starts with a lure, and each control in its path sees only part of the attack:

Email security: Half of the attacks we see never touch email. The lure arrives through a search ad, a chat message, social media, a calendar invite, or a QR code. The rest come from trusted senders and services, so they pass reputation checks.

Web gateways: The pages sit on trusted hosting and are assembled in the browser. The domains rotate every few days, so reputation data lags behind them.

Safe browsing and scanners: Bot checks and cloaking show scanners a harmless page. A new domain isn't on any blocklist yet.

How a phishing attack gets past email, URL, DNS, web gateway, and scanner controls before it reaches the user in the browser.

When the page loads in the user's browser and the user interacts with it, that's a breakthrough. Breakthrough rate counts those attacks, not attempts.

This changes how to read upstream data. A kit with a high breakthrough rate is one that upstream controls are missing. A low count in email or proxy logs doesn't prove that a kit is rare, because the kit may be getting past those controls without a trace.

Our upcoming webinar reveals the five kits with the highest breakthrough rates. Here's an early look at the number one kit.

From August to October 2026, one kit ranked first by breakthrough rate every month. DOMDIFFER, an AiTM phishing kit that targets corporate Google and Microsoft accounts, broke through 2-4x as often as the next kit each month. DOM mirroring, the mechanism it uses under the hood, also happens to be the newest and fastest-growing way for a kit to relay a sign-in.

We first saw DOMDIFFER in February 2026. DOMDIFFER is our name for the kit (it hasn't yet been linked to a known phishing-as-a-service brand). We believe it grew out of NakedPages, a reverse proxy kit, and the two kits share infrastructure in several places. DOMDIFFER went quiet in the spring, came back over the summer, and has held the top rating since August. Most of its detections in that time came from fake calendar event lures.

New hostnames per month for three NakedPages variants and DOMDIFFER, from our threat intelligence.

One real DOMDIFFER attack starts with a fake Google Voice notification about a new voicemail.

The lure for one DOMDIFFER attack: A fake Google Voice voicemail notification.

The link passes a bot check that turns scanners away. The victim then sees what looks exactly like Google's sign-in page. It isn't a screenshot or a static copy. It's Google's real page, mirrored from the attacker's browser.

Google's sign-in page, mirrored from the attacker's browser by DOMDIFFER.

On the surface, this looks like fairly standard phishing: A notification lure, a bot check gate, then a sign-in page. What makes DOMDIFFER particularly effective lies beneath the surface.

items.title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach
items.summary: Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. "While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a
items.details:
1Password says an attacker stole customer account data and source code via a compromised employee GitHub account, but vaults were unaffected.

Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

"While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said.

It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts.

As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including -

Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning , and account recovery

Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers

1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

"The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security."

"Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."

items.title: Drupal Warns of New Highly Critical Site Takeover Vulnerability Under Active Exploitation
items.summary: Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states
items.details:
Drupal patches an actively exploited core flaw that could allow site takeover on certain sites with remotely accessible installers.

Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states that could still be abused to facilitate site takeover even after the fix.

CVE-2026-132165 "recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer," Drupal maintainers said . "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites."

"It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state."

Drupal acknowledged that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, but emphasized that site owners who have already secured the installer ("install.php") are not impacted.

Specifically, any website that left its installer remotely accessible following the fix for CVE-2026-132165 may have been compromised. Drupal is urging site administrators to take the following actions -

Check site logs for unauthorized access, including unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account

Ensure the user 1 email address is set to under their control, and consider resetting user 1's password.

The issue has been remediated in the following versions -

After updating to the latest supported versions, it's recommended to run "update.php" to fix existing production sites in this state and secure the Drupal installer on all new and existing sites.

According to statistics shared by StepSecurity, there are about 55,800 internet-facing Drupal sites as of November 26, 2026, out of which 31,500 services are running branches that are vulnerable to CVE-2026-132165 and roughly 15,000 are on the end-of-life 8 and 9 branches.

items.details:
CISA adds 10 exploited flaws to its KEV catalog, including five in Mitel MiCollab, and warns of an unpatched Danfoss controller flaw.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added 10 security flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities ( KEV ) catalog, including five vulnerabilities impacting Mitel MiCollab that were disclosed last week.

CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An arbitrary file upload vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to upload arbitrary files to the target system.

CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score: 9.0) - An XML injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system.

CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score: 5.9) - An unauthorized access vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information.

CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score: 10.0) - A command injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system.

CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An authentication bypass vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication controls and perform unauthorized actions within the context of the application.

The issues affect MiCollab versions 10.3 and earlier. "Mitel provided a patch available for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) that addresses these vulnerabilities," the company said in an advisory published November 16, 2026. "Upgrade to this release and apply the provided patch, or upgrade to a later release."

Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. As of writing, there are currently no details on how the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild.

The addition comes against the backdrop of a report from Accenture's Apex Labs, which revealed that an unknown threat actor may have been weaponizing the flaws as zero-days as part of what's suspected to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted data theft campaign.

Evidence indicates the deployment of a web shell against one victim organization a day before Mitel released patches, only for the intrusion to progress rapidly and allowing the threat actor to harvest credentials and steal sensitive business data from a line-of-business database server within hours.

"At that victim, we found the threat actor ran its first command 12 minutes after its first request, then reached root on the MiCollab server within 30 minutes and used the directory credentials that MiCollab stores for its LDAP connector to authenticate to a domain controller within 32 minutes," Accenture said.

The activity is assessed to be part of a broader campaign targeting MiCollab instances, with a second organization's MiCollab server observed holding a persistent HTTPS channel to the threat actor infrastructure since November 9, 2026. It has not been established how this server was compromised as it had been found running an older MiCollab version affected by previously disclosed flaws (i.e., MTLVULN-1694 ).

"MiCollab presents an attractive target because it is commonly internet-facing and connected to critical enterprise services, including Active Directory," Accenture said. "Its history of exploitation further underscores this risk."

CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper validation of specified type of input vulnerability in Vates Xen Orchestra that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and perform actions with administrative privileges via a specially crafted authentication token containing an empty JSON object.

items.details:
13 malicious NuGet packages target Windows .NET developers through fake job assessments, using MSBuild and DLL sideloading to execute payloads.

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages that are designed to target Windows .NET developers under the guise of a fake take-home job assessment.

"Most of the packages pose as WinUI 3 and WPF [Windows Presentation Foundation] button controls," Socket security researcher Kush Pandya said in a technical write-up. "In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL sideloading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable."

All the identified NuGet packages have been deleted from the gallery as of writing. The names of the packages are listed below -

The first NuGet package, WinUI3IconButton, was uploaded to the registry on July 23, 2026, indicating that the campaign has been ongoing for quite some time without attracting attention. The last two uploads, HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls, occurred on November 4, 2026, after both VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls were removed by NuGet on November 2, 2026.

The starting point is a GitHub repository ("stevenleedig-ux/WinUI3_Home_Assessment") created on November 3, 2026. It features a set of assessment tasks revolving around enhancing a FileButton control and exception handling that candidates must implement within a span of three to four hours. It's unclear how targets are led to these decoy projects.

The README file also permits the test participants to use artificial intelligence (AI) development assistants like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, or Claude, but discourages them from copying and pasting the entire project into the tool and generating the solution without "understanding it."

Present within the assessment repository is a "WinUI3_Home_Assessment.csproj" file that references VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer version 1.2.7 and VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls version 1.0.7.

"VS_Builder.MSBuildAnalyzer, later republished as HappyOne.MSBuildAnalyzer, ships an MSBuild targets file, build/VS_Builder.MsBuildAnalyzer.targets, that runs a bundled DLL ['MSBuildAnalyzer.dll'] after every build," Pandya said. "In the version bundled with the lure, that DLL downloads a file from GitHub to %LOCALAPPDATA%\osk\OskSupport.dll and copies C:\Windows\System32\osk.exe next to it."

The VS_Builder.WinUI3Controls package then launches the copied binary via the FileButton control that "routes clicks to Windows files and folders," triggering the execution of the DLL via a known technique called DLL sideloading .

In a similar vein, creating a WUIButton control from the WinUI.Button package starts a background routine in "lib/net8.0-windows10.0.19041/WinUI.Button.dll" that downloads "avast.exe" from the "Carol-White-Super/cloud" repository via the GitHub API using an embedded access token, saves it as "%TEMP%\Launcher.exe," and runs it.

RevertButtonIcon and SetButtonColor "download a Windows executable to the user's temp folder and run it, and InitializeCustomButton starts the copy that SetButtonColor drops," Socket explained.

"Five more are tied to the set by dependency or by the lure: WinUI3IconButton (from version 1.1.4), StyledAppButton and StyledComponent depend on other packages in the set, WindowsAccentColorName is a dependency of SetButtonColor and InitializeCustomButton, and HappyOne.WinUI3Controls is the FileButton package the lure switched to."

Socket also said it identified two bogus repositories impersonating the axios JavaScript library -

stevenleedig-ux/axios-http (the same GitHub account hosting the assessment)

Both repositories have been flagged as copies of a malicious Node.js library named "axios-test-one" that impersonates the Axios HTTP client but contains functionality that enables code execution and shell access. The repositories serve a Windows executable named "lib/env/axios.csproj."

A loader ("updater.exe" and "msedgewebview2.exe") that uses a GitHub repository ("James-White-Super/React_prj") as a two-way command and control (C2)

items.title: USN-9203-1: libpcap vulnerabilities
items.summary: Jin Wei, Kunwei Qian, and Ping Chen discovered that libpcap did not properly validate the format of MAC addresses passed to the pcap_ether_aton() function, leading to an out-of-bounds read and write. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service, or possibly execute arbitrary code. This issue only affected Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. (CVE-2025-11961) It was discovered that the libpcap remote capture (rpcap) client did not properly validate packet messages received from the server. A malicious server could possibly use this issue to obtain sensitive information or cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-18238) It was discovered that the libpcap remote capture daemon (rpcapd) did not free memory allocated for filter programs received from clients. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause rpcapd to consume excessive memory, leading to a denial of service. (CVE-2026-18313) It was discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter incorrectly handled filter programs that contained invalid instructions. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-31911) It was discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter did not properly check the bounds of filter programs, leading to an out-of-bounds read. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service, or obtain sensitive information. (CVE-2026-31912) It was discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter did not check for division by zero in certain filter program instructions. An attacker could possibly use this issue to cause applications using libpcap to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-6244) Kaixuan Li discovered that the libpcap BPF interpreter did not limit the number of backward jumps in filter programs. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue with specially crafted network packets to cause applications using libpcap to stop responding, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-6554)

items.title: Palo Alto Networks warns of Fragnesia flaw exploited in PAN-OS attacks
items.summary: Threat actors are chaining exploits for the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to target Palo Alto Networks devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet. [...]
items.details:
Threat actors are chaining exploits for the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to target Palo Alto Networks devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet.

PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which allow unauthenticated attackers to run code remotely with the privileges of the PHP web worker.

The Fragnesia vulnerability , identified as CVE-2026-46300, is a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that lets a local attacker with low-privileges to escalate permissions to root level.

An alert from CISA on October 28 warned that both security issues were being chained in attacks to deploy PHP webshells on vulnerable systems and execute commands as root.

Around the same time, Dream Security researchers reported observing a campaign using the same chain, targeting servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including a U.S. government affiliate.

Palo Alto Networks has confirmed in an advisory today that such attacks also target firewalls running PAN-OS.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” reads the security bulletin .

The networking company says that all exploitation activity it observed involved PAN-OS devices that exposed their management interface to the public internet, which goes against its recommended ‘ best practices .’

Palo Alto Networks did not provide any technical details about the chaining of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, but noted that this is the only known way to exploit Fragnesia, and they are not aware of another exploitation pathway for the flaw.

The company has released fixes for Fragnesia for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2, with the exact patch-carrying build varying by release.

Given that the two flaws are exploited together, administrators who applied updates that addressed the PHP2Shell flaw should be safe from these attacks.

In addition to applying the security updates, Palo Alto Networks also recommends that those who need to keep a remote management interface available restrict access to trusted internal IP addresses.

items.title: 1Password customer data stolen after employee GitHub account breach
items.summary: 1Password has disclosed a data breach after a an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data. [...]
items.details:
1Password has disclosed a data breach after a an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.

1Password has disclosed a data breach after an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data.

The company says customer password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised in the attack.

In a security incident disclosure published today, 1Password says it began investigating the breach on November 19 after detecting indications that an employee's GitHub account had been compromised.

The attacker used the account to access private source code repositories and inject malicious code into backend services that downloaded customer account records.

The attacker also stole internal company source code and accessed its continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environment, potentially exposing internal infrastructure credentials.

Among the stolen customer data were tokens embedded in links that 1Password emailed to users to accept account provisioning invitations or recover their accounts.

However, 1Password says these tokens cannot be used on their own to access customer accounts, as completing the invitation or recovery process requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address.

The company says only a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified.

As a precaution against brute-force attacks, 1Password has strengthened these verification codes from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters.

The company says it has now disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services, and rotated or revoked potentially exposed infrastructure credentials.

1Password has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its remediation efforts and says it has found no internal evidence of customer account takeovers.

The company is not requiring customers to change their account passwords or Secret Keys but warns them to watch for unexpected invitations, account recovery requests, and other potential phishing attempts.

While customer vaults were not compromised in the attack, the stolen data is valuable to threat actors as it provides a list of known 1Password users who could be targeted in phishing campaigns.

Threat actors could send emails impersonating 1Password, using the breach as a lure to trick customers into disclosing their account passwords, Secret Keys, or recovery verification codes.

Customers should be particularly wary of emails claiming they need to secure their accounts in response to the breach, reset their passwords, or verify their account information.

Rather than clicking on links in these emails, customers should access their accounts directly through the 1Password website or app and never share their passwords, Secret Keys, or verification codes with anyone.

BleepingComputer contacted 1Password with questions about the attack but has not yet received a response.

items.title: CVE-2026-134070 - Improper input sanitization in the AWS Config remediation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-203-AWS Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST Description: AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document. We identified CVE-2026-134070, where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions. Impacted versions: Revisions created before 2026-10-22 (UTC) Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-203-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST

AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document.

We identified CVE-2026-134070 , where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions.

Impacted versions: Revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC)

This issue has been addressed in a fixed revision of the AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3, available in all Regions where the runbook is available. The fixed revision is the latest revision in each Region. Its revision number varies by Region. To find it, run: aws ssm describe-document --name AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 --region <region> --query "Document.LatestVersion" We recommend upgrading to the latest revision and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. Update any Automation executions, State Manager associations, AWS Config remediation configurations, or other automations pinned to an earlier revision to use the latest revision.

Any user permitted to run the runbook can choose which revision to run. Earlier revisions remain runnable until AWS deprecates all revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC), beginning January 15, 2027, in every Region and partition. Until then, follow the protection described under Workarounds, and confirm that all invocation paths use the latest revision.

The fixed runbook updates only the S3 bucket and prefix fields of an existing Session Manager preferences document, so any settings injected before you updated remain in place. You need to review a Region only if your Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) was first created there by an earlier revision of this runbook, not by you. To check: Look for any run of this runbook that failed with "DOCUMENT CREATE OR UPDATE FAILED." An injected run always fails with this error. Find when the document was first created by running aws ssm list-document-versions --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell --region <region> and noting the CreatedDate of the first version. If that date matches a run of this runbook, the runbook created the document. To view the current settings, run aws ssm get-document --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell --region <region> --query Content --output text. Repeat this check in each Region where you use Session Manager. Look for settings you did not configure, especially: shellProfile: commands that run at the start of every session, runAsEnabled and runAsDefaultUser: the operating system user that sessions run as, maxSessionDuration and idleSessionTimeout, the logging destination fields (s3BucketName, s3KeyPrefix, cloudWatchLogGroupName, kmsKeyId).

If you find any, restore your trusted preferences and review instances on which Session Manager sessions were started while those settings were active.

Until AWS removes earlier revisions in your Region, do one of the following:

Keep untrusted users from running earlier revisions of the runbook.

Keep a trusted Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) in every Region. Earlier revisions inject only when they create this document, so while a trusted one exists, this path is closed in that Region.

Keep this protection in place until earlier revisions are removed. Also complete the review described under "Review your Session Manager preferences".

We would like to thank k4ddy for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.title: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks
items.summary: Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector. [...]
items.details:
Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector.

The two agencies listed four AI-powered penetration testing and red-teaming frameworks that have been involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents : ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness - Red Team, and PentAGI.

Both agencies have urged organizations to reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet, prioritize patching, and monitor for unusual activity.

CSIRT Italia says it detected large-scale malicious campaigns that used autonomous AI agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on exposed endpoints.

In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours.

In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence.

The agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks.

“During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low-impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says .

“They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.”

The Italian cybersecurity agency advises administrators to prioritize patching internet-facing systems, focus on addressing flaws known to be actively exploited in the wild, and disable remote management interfaces if not needed.

The agency also recommends monitoring control plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic to detect suspicious activity.

Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) warned of similar campaigns targeting organizations in the country, confirming the first cases of successful AI-assisted cyberattacks.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said .

“Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

“In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.”

The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next.

NCSC says that the number of AI agents publicly (and often freely) available to cybercriminals has nearly doubled since October, resulting in these massive waves against Swiss organizations, including critical infrastructure operators.

items.title: Oh, is it Thanksgiving? I hadn’t noticed!
items.summary: In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors).
items.details:
In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors).

I tried hard not to write another typical “Thanksgiving article.” Obviously, I failed. But you know what? It is Thanksgiving week here in the U.S., and coming up with fun, interesting, short form topics is hard , especially when you’re fighting the weight of Tradition expected this week. So instead of me writing something insightful, you’re getting some things I’m thankful for. Even that’s harder than you might think, because there are so many things, and this is just the newsletter introduction , after all.

Let’s start off with something I’m pretty sure none of us are thankful for: threat actors. Seriously, screw you guys! I know I'd be out of a job without you, but that’s just another way of saying “I coulda been a professional bagpiper.” There are days when that doesn’t sound so bad. So, no gratitude coming your way, people!

In terms of actual thankfulness, I want to give a big THANK YOU to the entire Blue Team, everywhere. Everyone out there defending, especially those in the U.S. taking shifts on Thursday to keep the turkey-eating public safe and secure. This is a hard, often high-pressure job for which you get little thanks, but all the blame when a breach occurs. We see you. We appreciate you. We promise we’ll save you some stuffing.

Speaking of defenders, I’m also very thankful to get to work with so many talented and wonderful people here at Talos. I’m not just saying this because I know my boss will read it! Without exception, everyone I’ve worked with here has not only been an expert at what they do, but they’ve been friendly, welcoming, and very patient with me as I’ve been feeling my way around this new org over the past several months. Thank you!

Finally, and maybe most importantly of all, I want to thank you , our readers. You are the reason we’re all here, doing what we do, helping you to look out for your own networks and protect your own people. We appreciate your trust!

Whether you’re celebrating Thanksgiving here in the States or just having a normal weekend wherever you are, I hope you get some time to relax, unplug, recharge, and de-stress.

In Talos’ latest blog , we examine the fascinating tradecraft of the OpenAI-linked agentic swarm that broke out of its containerized environment in 2026. While not inherently malicious, this swarm of AI agents used public internet services as improvised infrastructure to bypass their sandbox constraints and complete their training tasks. By analyzing this unintentional great escape, we can learn how multi-agent systems coordinate, partition work, and adapt when their paths are blocked. This view into autonomous AI operations provides a baseline for understanding how these behaviors transfer to purpose-built cyber attack frameworks.

The leap from an AI sandbox escape to weaponized cyber attacks has already happened. Agentic frameworks like ARTEX are currently in the wild, proving that multi-agent systems can move from a single compromised credential to deep network access in under 15 minutes. These autonomous threats adapt to errors in real time and execute dozens of actions in mere seconds. Understanding how these swarms coordinate, adapt, and exfiltrate data is a necessity to keep up with an adversary that operates at machine speed.

To catch an AI swarm, defenders must look for its operational fingerprints. Monitor your environment for irregular "burst-and-pause" timing patterns that indicate rapid, sub-second automated reasoning. Keep a close eye on unusual traffic to allow-listed public services like “webhook.site”, which agents use to park data before terminating. Finally, hunt for self-labeling conventions, like highly specific URL parameters or predictable file names (e.g., “artex-probe-*”), that agents rely on to track their state. Read the full blog for a deeper dive into these swarm behaviors.

AI-assisted cyber attacks trigger unauthorized payments at Indian banks and fintech firms The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned the attacks have resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts. ( The Hacker News )

JPMorgan, Visa confirm customer data taken in third-party vendor hacks Marketing data, including email addresses, were affected. Both Visa and JPMorgan said the incidents were unrelated to tech disruptions reported earlier this week. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

OpenAI and Cisco unveil AI-assisted Linux security tool to block exploits before patching OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows AI agents to defend systems without downtime. ( The Hacker News )

AI-enabled campaign targets Check Point Security Management servers The attacks led to at least 22 organizations being compromised across the globe, including in the UK, the U.S., France, Germany, Australia, China, India and Australia. The targeted organizations work in the energy, transportation, financial services and government sectors. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

Drupal Fail2Install exploit details emerge as critical RCE flaw faces active exploitation While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources. ( The Hacker News )

Beers with Talos: Ranksgiving with guest Anton Chuvakin This Ranksgiving, Dave has a brand new (though no less controversial) topic: the top five kitchen utensils/gadgets needed to make Thanksgiving dinner. Prepare to be both aghast and disappointed (as usual) in the team's choices.

UAT-12643 blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing Talos discovered UAT-12643 using Overlord RAT, which implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos.

Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security.
