items.details:
GitHub Actions attackers exploited SHA pinning trust gaps to disguise malicious commits, while new workflow lockfiles leave provenance risks unresolve

Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning . If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

Led by Erika Heidi , Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard , the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

items.title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity
items.summary: A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday. The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked
items.details:
Google Project Zero details how .NET Framework loading behavior enabled local security bypasses in VirtualBox and Windows, both patched.

A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268 , and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398 .

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking . He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis .

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE.

On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it.

.NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694.

items.details:
2027 SOC Budget Reset: 5 Priorities to Cut Costs and Reduce Cyber Risk | Read more hacking news on The Hacker News cybersecurity news website and learn how to protect against cyberattacks and software vulnerabilities.

What if your biggest SOC budget problem isn't how much you spend, but how much analyst time you lose?

According to ANY.RUN 's estimates, SOC teams could recover 450 analyst hours per 1,000 investigated alerts through faster threat analysis and IOC research. That's a significant opportunity as manual investigations, repeated checks, and unnecessary escalations continue to drain resources.

As 2027 approaches, here are five priorities to reduce SOC costs, recover capacity, and strengthen protection against costly cyberattacks.

Cybersecurity spending is facing conflicting pressures. According to IANS and Artico Search, 55% of CISOs reported flat or declining budgets in 2026 . Meanwhile, PwC's 2027 Global Digital Trust Insights found that 84% of surveyed security and finance leaders expect cybersecurity budgets to increase .

Growing workloads: More alerts and complex threats demand additional investigation capacity.

Rising operational costs: Manual processes, staffing needs, and expanding security infrastructure put pressure on budgets.

Pressure to prove ROI: Every investment must demonstrate measurable improvements in security and operational efficiency.

Increasing cyber risks: Cost reductions cannot come at the expense of detection coverage or response capabilities.

AI is becoming a major cybersecurity investment priority, but adding AI capabilities won't automatically improve SOC efficiency. For 2027, the focus should be on reducing investigation costs, improving analyst productivity, and avoiding unnecessary escalations.

For example, ANY.RUN's Interactive Sandbox combines automated threat analysis with AI-powered reporting to help teams achieve these goals:

Cut manual investigation time: Automated Interactivity follows redirects, extracts QR code links, and handles supported CAPTCHAs, exposing malicious activity that would otherwise require additional analyst effort.

ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox automatically solves CAPTCHA, revealing full attack chain

Reduce investigation and escalation costs: AI-powered Tier 1 reports provide clear summaries of malicious behavior and recommended next steps. This helps analysts make faster decisions and reduces the need for repeated investigations and unnecessary Tier 2 involvement.

AI-powered Tier 1 report with attack summary and recommendations for faster handoffs

These improvements have measurable business value. ANY.RUN reports up to 20% lower Tier 1 workload and 30% fewer Tier 1-to-Tier 2 escalations , helping SOCs handle growing workloads with less pressure to expand their teams.

The 2027 budget priority: Evaluate AI investments based on investigation time, workload reduction, and escalation rates, not the number of AI features included.

Reduce Tier 1 workload by up to 20% and control investigation costs.

As alert volumes grow, hiring additional analysts may seem like the obvious solution. But before expanding headcount, SOCs should calculate how much capacity they could recover by improving investigation efficiency.

Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. items.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

items.summary: View CSAF Summary Schneider Electric is aware of a vulnerability in its EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody product. The EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody is used to enter or import the single line diagram, to get the extensive bill of material of your switchboard, including all devices, connection items, and mounting components. items.title: Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series
items.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges. The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected: AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 (CVE-2026-129713) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Danfoss AK-SM8xxA 1 Vulnerability Stack-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Denmark Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-129713 A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. Read More 1 Affected Product Danfoss AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation This vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases. Mitigation Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overview Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-121 Stack-based Buffer Overflow CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 9.3 CRITICAL CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . items.title: Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster: defending against agentic cyber attacks
items.summary: How to protect your organisation from cyber attacks created using ‘agentic offensive frameworks’.
items.details:
How to protect your organisation from cyber attacks created using ‘agentic offensive frameworks’.

Since September 2026, the NCSC has seen a marked rise in AI-assisted cyber attacks. Organisations across multiple sectors are reporting incidents as a result of threat actors using ‘agentic offensive frameworks'; software originally designed for red teaming being applied beyond its defensive purpose.

The incidents involved automated identification and exploitation attempts across organisations' internet-facing services and assets in quick succession. This resulted in downtime to some services or the compromise of systems, providing attackers with a foothold for further agent-driven activity (or in some cases, human-driven activity within their network).

none of the weaknesses being exploited are new or novel

the tools the agents have access to are common and provide no new capability the typical threat actor would have access to

What has changed, is how quickly and persistently threat actors can conduct attacks – at low cost – using these frameworks combined with cheap, capable open models or illegal API resellers.

This blog explains how agentic offensive frameworks are being used, what this means for cyber defenders, and the steps you should take to help protect your organisation.

An agentic offensive framework allows AI models to interact with a set of off-the-shelf cyber security tools for the purpose of probing digital systems for weaknesses. Typically, a framework will:

At the time of writing (November 2026), this type of activity has become synonymous with the ARTEX framework, a multi-agent penetration testing and red-teaming tool originally developed for authorised security testing. Different tools come and go (others include Cairn, PentAGI, RedAmon, Xalgorix and Darkmoon), so rather than concentrating on a particular framework, here we’ll focus on how the combination of a human attacker plus a capable model plus a framework creates an uplift in capability.

Compared with a human attacker working without tools, an agent plus a framework:

works quickly (it moves from discovery to exploitation in minutes)

is exhaustive in its search (it will try every endpoint, parameter and credential it finds)

instantly learns from failures (it creates memory, reads error messages, responds and adapts its next attempt)

is cheap to run, at scale (the cost of running automated attacks is low)

This does mean that today's frameworks are noisy. They trade stealth for speed, generate a lot of traffic and will interact with almost anything they find, which makes them easier to detect . This may not always be the case if future frameworks prioritise stealth.

Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated. Once an initial foothold has been gained, the agents explore the environment, exploiting the fact that many credentials in an organisation are over-privileged for their needs, and networks are often flat or interconnected.

Organisations need strong operational discipline to avoid being overwhelmed by the volume, intensity and duration of attacks from agentic offensive frameworks. Answering the following questions will help you develop a holistic approach that can protect your organisation.

items.title: Introducing CORNERSTONE: delivering external services for the NCSC
items.summary: The NCSC is seeking industry feedback on a new delivery model for modernising external cyber security services.
items.details:
The NCSC is seeking industry feedback on a new delivery model for modernising external cyber security services.

The NCSC's existing services have developed strong standards, trusted market relationships and significant reach. But as demand grows, we need to consider how these services can be delivered in ways that are scalable, sustainable, and responsive to the UK’s changing needs.

As a result, the NCSC is exploring how it can modernise the way its external services are designed, delivered and developed. We want to create an operating model that enables NCSC services to achieve greater impact, reach more organisations, respond more quickly to changing threats and technology, and make better use of the capabilities that exist across the cyber security industry.

CORNERSTONE is a multi-year project to develop a more scalable relationship between the NCSC and industry, with each focusing on where it can add most value. Our ambition for CORNERSTONE is not simply to outsource services currently run by the NCSC; we want to make our services more impactful, accessible and adaptable. This will allow the NCSC to focus on those areas where it brings unique insight as the national technical authority for cyber security.

We want organisations with cyber security expertise and real-world experience of assurance and service delivery to challenge our thinking before any future competition. More specifically, we are seeking feedback on a proposal which sees industry partners delivering the following NCSC services:

Currently, CHECK and CRTF are distinct assurance schemes operated with significant NCSC involvement, while the existing PDNS contract is a different kind of service altogether. The proposed new PDNS assurance scheme would create something new rather than simply transfer the existing PDNS service into the arrangement.

The purpose of bringing these areas together is to explore whether there are common administrative, data and operating capabilities that can be provided more effectively. These could include:

providing common tools and infrastructure where appropriate

Meaningful market engagement depends on hearing from organisations with real-world experience of cyber security assurance and operating at scale. We therefore encourage you to read the accompanying Market Engagement Prospectus (PDF) , and provide feedback on the commercial and practical viability of our assumptions. These include:

this phase of CORNERSTONE will operate as a self-funding concession model

the NCSC will remain the root of trust for badging and assuring schemes and services

the NCSC will remain the owner of the NCSC-assured brand

organisations will work collaboratively with the NCSC to bring together expertise to deliver innovative new schemes and services

delivery partners will work in accordance with our security requirements for managing and storing data

delivery partners will ensure services are able to respond at pace to the changing technological and geopolitical environment

We’re hosting two identical Supplier Information Sessions over MS Teams on 2nd December and 9th December, 10:00 – 11:00. During these meetings, we will talk through our plans and provide an opportunity for interested organisations to hear more about CORNERSTONE. Questions and answers from these sessions will be captured and made available to all interested parties. You can register your place by clicking on one of the dates below:

We anticipate beginning the tender process in Spring 2027 and are considering a contract length of around five years. However, our longer-term ambition for CORNERSTONE is broader than the initial three services described above. We intend to explore a scalable operating model through which the NCSC can govern, assure and enable a wider portfolio of external services, including both cyber assurance and Active Cyber Defence services, where industry delivery is appropriate.

In the meantime, we welcome thoughts, comments and questions by 18th December at [email protected] .

items.details:
Microsoft fixed an Azure API Management Classic flaw that could expose secrets in improperly secured instances as an unknown actor sought credentials.

Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) has disclosed that it became aware of a security vulnerability in Microsoft's Azure API Management (APIM) that has affected multiple businesses in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi .

"An unknown actor has been actively looking for access tokens, secrets, and named values ​​in APIM," NSM said . "It is still uncertain how extensive the exploitation of the vulnerability is, and has been."

The security agency said it has so far seen no evidence that has had any impact on Norwegian businesses.

According to a non-public advisory issued by Microsoft, the issue is said to affect the APIM classic tier. Instances on v2 tiers are not affected.

"On 18 November 2026, Microsoft identified a security issue affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices," Microsoft said in the advisory.

"Microsoft closed the access path on 19 November 2026. Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue."

As a result, credentials or configuration secrets associated with the API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized third-party if the service has not been configured as per security best practices. The information that may have been accessed could include -

Secrets stored in Named Values Client secrets associated with identity providers

Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers

As of November 21, 2026, the Windows maker has released guidance for customers to help identify and rotate the secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects," security researcher Anders Kristiansen said . "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid."

NSM has also warned that the vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and other entities outside of the country, adding it's working with national and international partners and businesses about the matter.

items.title: WHMCS SQL Injection Could Expose Customer Data and Admin Password Hashes without Login
items.summary: A flaw in WHMCS's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed. The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released
items.details:
WHMCS fixes an unauthenticated SQL injection that could expose customer records and admin password hashes, along with two other vulnerabilities.

A flaw in WHMCS 's shopping cart, the billing and automation platform many web hosting companies use to run their businesses, could allow anyone on the internet to retrieve customer records and administrator password hashes from an installation's database. No login is needed.

The company disclosed the SQL injection yesterday along with two other flaws that need a logged-in client, and released fixed versions. It has not reported attacks using any of the three.

Because no login is needed, the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-82981 (CVSS score: 8.7), is within reach of anyone who can load the shopping cart of a vulnerable installation over the internet.

The records an attacker could pull include clients' personal and support information as well as admin accounts with their hashed passwords, according to the company's advisory. A stolen hash is not a working password, but it gives attackers something to try to crack offline.

The 9.0.10 and 8.13.8 updates shipped yesterday, and the release notes list them as maintenance releases. For the 9.1 series, the security advisory names 9.1.2 as the fix, but that build had not yet appeared on the company's 9.1 release notes page at publication time.

Fixes are available only for supported versions, so installations on the 8.0 to 8.12 series must upgrade to a fixed release.

Installing the updates falls to self-hosted administrators, since WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, according to the company's updating documentation .

The second SQL injection, CVE-2026-82979 (CVSS score: 7.1), sits in the Client Area and needs a logged-in client that holds the View & Manage Contacts permission. That client could read other customers' personal, billing, and support information, as well as the same admin records and password hashes, the second advisory says.

The third flaw, CVE-2026-93700 , lies in how email campaigns process client-supplied data. A logged-in client could use it to read sensitive configuration files on the server, including database credentials, and to run code on the server, its advisory says.

It carries the highest score of the three, 9.0, though its CVE record uses the older CVSS 3.1 scale while the other two use CVSS 4.0. That record's vector indicates that some user interaction is required, and the company has not said what else exploitation entails.

All three flaws were reported by a single researcher who uses the handle alakazamspooon .

For the email-campaign flaw, updating is not the whole job. The email-campaign advisory also tells administrators to:

Delete every planned or ongoing campaign under Utilities > Email Campaigns, using Delete in each campaign's Manage Campaign menu.

Clear the template cache under Utilities > System > System Cleanup, using Empty Template Cache.

The advisory does not explain why existing campaigns must go, leaving open the question of whether updating alone is enough.

This is at least the third round of WHMCS security fixes this year. The company patched an authorization flaw in the Client Area on May 12, described in its May advisory , and an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw on September 3, described in its September advisory .

items.details:
OpenAI and Cisco launch Shirudo, an open-source Linux runtime that uses AI-generated eBPF shields to mitigate exploits without service downtime.

OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.

"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.

The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.

The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.

Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.

The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.

To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.

"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said . "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."

Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon , an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.

Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.

"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

An agent is tasked with finding new vulnerabilities in an application, or working off external sources of new vulnerability disclosures.

Shirudo on the operator machine builds a security shield consisting of eBPF or application bytecode after reproducing and validating the exploit.

The shield is delivered as signed .bee packages via an OCI-compliant registry.

The Shirudo layer on each target pulls these .bee packages, validating each signature using TPMs to establish trust and safety.

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.

OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.

"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."

items.title: Hackers Exploit N-able MailAssure Flaw While AI Agents Exploit MONAI Label Zero-Day
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The critical vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP
items.details:
CISA flags two exploited N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label flaws, including a zero-day AI agents used to gain root shell access.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added two flaws impacting N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities ( KEV ) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able MailAssure's LDAP synchronization connection check that could allow an authenticated API user to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.

CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution.

The exploitation of CVE-2026-134624 stems from a disclosure last week, in which N-able said it detected a security incident that resulted in a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

As of November 21, 2026, 11:44 p.m. UTC, access to the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud dashboard and APIs has been restored.

"N-able has remediated the recent security incident affecting our Mail Assure and SpamExperts environments and restored the impacted functionality," a spokesperson for the company told The Hacker News. Our investigation to date indicates that exploitation was confined to a single N-able hosted server and continued monitoring since remediation has found no further malicious activity."

CVE-2026-133968, on the other hand, has been linked to an agentic attack in which a suspected China-nexus threat actor leveraged CAIRN , an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered problem-solving engine, to conduct hacking operations with minimal human involvement.

The activity, which ran for an approximately 48-hour period beginning September 8, 2026, targeted IP addresses associated with universities across East Asia outside mainland China.

"In this campaign, the actor provided a list of targeted IP addresses with variations of the goal to 'obtain shell access,'" CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said. "Based on those inputs, the AI agents planned, executed, and adjusted their approach as they learned, without the operator choosing each next step."

Some of these attacks unsuccessfully attempted to brute-force their way into a Redis instance at one university and a GPU server at another. The activity also singled out an unspecified target running MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application, identifying the aforementioned zero-day and exploiting it in about 11 minutes to write arbitrary files to the server.

"In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup," Moses said. "The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root."

Following the discovery of the zero-day, the operator is said to have provided the AI agents with a proxy to tunnel into a second university network running the same vulnerable software, and then directed them to target other machines in that network.

The attacks are part of a broader cluster of attacks involving the use of AI-driven frameworks like ARTEX , CAIRN , and AntiFox , and CyberStrikeAI in recent months. A subset of these activities is estimated to have breached over 100 companies, including John Deere and SharkNinja. The end goals, per NorForge , revolve around establishing persistent access and financial theft -

AIA0001, which has targeted organizations, mainly in the U.S., Japan, and Australia, to deploy web shells and gain access to e-commerce and payment infrastructure for subsequent monetization.

AIA0002, which has targeted merchant payment services, gray-market payment sites, pharmaceutical sites, and a criminal carding site for financial gain.

AIA0003, which has targeted smaller e-commerce sites and very large U.S.-based commercial platforms to obtain shell access, admin panel access, or database access.

In a report published last week, Amazon Web Services (AWS) also revealed that its MadPot sensor network captured requests from AI agents linked to two offensive campaigns running on ARTEX, an AI-native penetration framework.

"The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting," AWS said . "Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection."

The system must be rebooted for this update to take effect.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Retroactive CVE assignments are always documented in the corresponding errata and on Red Hat's CVE pages. We strongly advise against delaying updates, as doing so may leave your system exposed when protections are already available.

items.title: CVE-2026-134069 - Use of a default cryptographic key in the instance registration of Amazon SSM Agent on AWS Windows Server AMIs
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-197-AWS Publication Date: 11/23/2026 13:30 PM PST Description: Amazon SSM Agent is the AWS Systems Manager agent that runs on EC2 instances so they can be managed through Systems Manager. We identified CVE-2026-134069, an issue in Amazon SSM Agent on AWS-provided Windows Server AMIs released before 2026-09-09, where instances launched from the same AMI shared one instance registration key. On instances managed through Default Host Management Configuration, a local user without administrative privileges might be able to obtain the instance's Default Host Management Configuration role credentials. Impacted versions: Amazon SSM Agent < 3.3.5226.0 on AWS Windows Server AMIs released before 2026-09-09. Instances launched from these AMIs remain affected after an in-place agent upgrade. Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Learn about CVE-2026-134069, a default key issue in Amazon SSM Agent on AWS Windows Server AMIs. Update now to ensure security. - AWS

Bulletin ID: 2026-197-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/23/2026 13:30 PM PST

Amazon SSM Agent is the AWS Systems Manager agent that runs on EC2 instances so they can be managed through Systems Manager.

We identified CVE-2026-134069 , an issue in Amazon SSM Agent on AWS-provided Windows Server AMIs released before 2026-09-09, where instances launched from the same AMI shared one instance registration key. On instances managed through Default Host Management Configuration, a local user without administrative privileges might be able to obtain the instance's Default Host Management Configuration role credentials.

Amazon SSM Agent < 3.3.5226.0 on AWS Windows Server AMIs released before 2026-09-09. Instances launched from these AMIs remain affected after an in-place agent upgrade.

This issue has been addressed in Amazon SSM Agent version 3.3.5226.0 , included in AWS Windows Server AMIs released on or after 2026-09-09. Instances launched from an affected AMI keep the shared key after an in-place agent upgrade, so we recommend replacing them with instances launched from these AMIs. Deleting the agent's Vault is not a supported remediation and breaks instances managed through Default Host Management Configuration.

If you cannot replace affected instances immediately, limit local, non-administrative user access on Amazon SSM Agent instances that are managed through Default Host Management Configuration and were launched from an affected AMI.

We would like to thank The YOSS Platform for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.title: CVE-2026-134056 - Out-of-bounds write in padded block cipher decryption in AWS-LC
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-196-AWS Publication Date: 11/23/2026 12:00 PM PST Description: We identified CVE-2026-134056, an out-of-bounds write issue in AWS-LC's padded block cipher decryption. It affects applications that decrypt CBC or ECB ciphertext with PKCS7 padding over multiple update calls. If the output buffer is the minimum documented size, AWS-LC can write one byte past its end. This might crash the application or corrupt adjacent memory. This issue does not disclose data. The aws-lc-rs StreamingDecryptingKey API has a similar issue with cbc_pkcs7 and ecb_pkcs7. Its less_safe_update function can write up to one block (16 bytes for AES) past the buffer. Single-call decryption is not affected. Neither is decryption without padding, nor modes such as CTR, CFB, and GCM. Customers of AWS services do not need to take action. Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-196-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/23/2026 12:00 PM PST

AWS-LC is an open-source, general-purpose cryptographic library.

We identified CVE-2026-134056, an out-of-bounds write issue in AWS-LC's padded block cipher decryption. It affects applications that decrypt CBC or ECB ciphertext with PKCS7 padding over multiple update calls. If the output buffer is the minimum documented size, AWS-LC can write one byte past its end. This might crash the application or corrupt adjacent memory. This issue does not disclose data. The aws-lc-rs StreamingDecryptingKey API has a similar issue with cbc_pkcs7 and ecb_pkcs7. Its less_safe_update function can write up to one block (16 bytes for AES) past the buffer.

Single-call decryption is not affected. Neither is decryption without padding, nor modes such as CTR, CFB, and GCM.

AWS-LC-FIPS 1.x is affected and reached end of support in October 2026.

This issue has been addressed in the following versions:

We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Applications are not affected if they decrypt in a single update call. They are also not affected if the output buffer is at least the input length plus one block. Otherwise, there is no workaround. Upgrade to a fixed version. AWS-LC-FIPS 1.x reached end of support in October 2026 and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to a supported, fixed AWS-LC-FIPS release.

We would like to thank dywzju09 for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any security questions or concerns.

items.title: Webworm Suspected of Modifying SoftEther VPN to Evade Detection and Hide Remote Access
items.summary: The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks. The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools,"
items.details:
Rapid7 links a stealth-focused SoftEther VPN Bridge variant to Webworm with moderate confidence, detailing changes designed to evade detection.

The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks.

The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence.

First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations.

One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN , with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable (" netcapa.exe "), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The mutated version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026.

"The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions."

The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN."

One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity.

It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response.

The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark.

Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below -

Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB.

Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII.

What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth.

"It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools.

"We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."
